findings.summary: A defined non-blind reviewer role is omitted from the producer set
findings.detail: PRODUCER_ROLES excludes OPTIONAL_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEWER, although CP-HI-04 includes every non-blind reviewer. Call sequence: bind session S as OPTIONAL_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEWER for run R → bind S as BLIND_REVIEWER for R → assertReviewerIndependence queries only PRODUCER_ROLES and allows S. The production gate later uses the same incomplete check, so this can admit non-independent blind-review evidence.
findings.suggestedFix: Include OPTIONAL_ADVERSARIAL_REVIEWER in the producer classification and make role classification exhaustive so every newly added role must explicitly be classified as producer or non-producer.

findings.summary: Final CEO independence ignores the normal project-scoped Primary CTO binding
findings.detail: assertFinalCeoIndependence relies on byRun, which only selects assignments carrying the run ID or one of its task IDs. A normal PRIMARY_CTO assignment is project-scoped and has run_id=null. Call sequence: bind project P's Primary CTO to session S → dispatch run R and pin S as owner → assertFinalCeoIndependence(R, S). The method finds no conflicting assignment and returns allow, permitting the run's CTO session to act as final CEO contrary to CP-HI-04.
findings.suggestedFix: Check the run's pinned owner session directly and retain an immutable run-specific producer/CTO relation. Continue checking all historical blind-review bindings for the run.

findings.summary: Caller-controlled role keys and scopes permit forged role bindings
findings.detail: bind and switchTo persist roleKey, role, projectId, runId, and taskId independently without verifying roleKeyFor(role, scope) or the role's required scope. For example, bind({roleKey:'PRIMARY_CTO:P', role:'CEO', projectId:null,...}) succeeds; role-key consumers treat the session as project P's CTO while role-based checks see a CEO. The inverse routes CEO traffic to a Primary CTO. Omitting runId for BLIND_REVIEWER also skips the independence check at line 61.
findings.suggestedFix: Derive roleKey inside BindingRegistry from a validated role-specific scope, reject missing or extraneous scope fields, and prevent a role key's semantic role/scope from changing across generations.

findings.summary: A binding switch can orphan every active run owned by the old generation
findings.detail: switchTo revokes the old binding, activates the successor, and commits without checking or updating runs pinned to the old owner tuple. Call sequence: dispatch R to session S1/generation 1 → switchTo S2/generation 2 → assertOwner(R,S1,1) rejects because generation 1 is revoked, while assertOwner(R,S2,2) rejects because R remains pinned to S1/1. Pending dispatches are nevertheless retargeted to S2. A crash before a separate reassignOwner call leaves the run permanently ownerless in practice, violating §11.1 and the mandatory owner-takeover transaction boundary.
findings.suggestedFix: Provide one atomic takeover operation that switches the binding and repoints every affected live run before commit. Refuse standalone switchTo when the current binding owns active runs; normal replacement must require zero active runs.

findings.summary: A caller can activate a STARTING session despite the mandatory READY failover precondition
findings.detail: The public allowStarting flag bypasses the READY check in both bind and switchTo. Call sequence: SessionRegistry.create() leaves session S in STARTING → switchTo(..., sessionId:S, allowStarting:true) → S becomes the active generation and pending messages are retargeted to it without readiness. This contradicts §15.7's required 'New Session READY' step.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove allowStarting from active binding operations. If startup needs a reservation, represent it separately and activate it only after the readiness transition succeeds.

findings.summary: Deliverable messages are selected but never atomically claimed
findings.detail: claimDeliverable performs a read-only SELECT and leaves every returned row PENDING; markSent later updates unconditionally. Two overlapping delivery loops therefore select and send the same message, contradicting §34.1. There is also a failover race: delivery reads an old-generation message → switchTo retargets the still-PENDING row to the new session → delivery sends its stale in-memory copy to the revoked session → markSent marks the retargeted database row SENT, falsely recording delivery to the new session and preventing its actual delivery.
findings.suggestedFix: Atomically transition selected rows to an IN_FLIGHT lease with a claim token. Coordinate failover with active claims, and make send/failure completion compare-and-set on the claim token, status, session, and generation.

findings.summary: An ACK from a revoked generation is accepted when it still matches the stored row
findings.detail: acknowledge compares only the supplied session/generation with the envelope fields. It never verifies that the assignment is still ACTIVE, that the message remains eligible, or that it has not expired. Call sequence: send message M to S1/generation 1 → switch the role to generation 2 while M is SENT → receive S1's late ACK → acknowledge marks M ACKED. Section 15.7 and §34.4 require that ACK to be audit-only. REJECTED and EXPIRED rows can likewise be overwritten as ACKED.
findings.suggestedFix: Within one transaction, verify the role's current active binding, message status, and expiry, then conditionally update the row. Audit and deny any revoked, expired, rejected, or otherwise stale ACK.

findings.summary: An idempotency-key collision silently suppresses a different message
findings.detail: When a key already exists, enqueue returns allow(OUTBOX_DUPLICATE_SUPPRESSED) without comparing role, generation, target, run, kind, or payload digest. Call sequence: enqueue key K with payload A → enqueue K with payload B or a different target/generation → the second call reports allowed but B is never queued. This is not an idempotent replay and can silently discard required dispatch intent.
findings.suggestedFix: Persist an immutable fingerprint of the original enqueue request. Return the existing message only when the fingerprint matches exactly; otherwise deny with OUTBOX_PAYLOAD_DIGEST_MISMATCH or CONFLICT.

findings.summary: Every delivery failure is retried immediately without failure classification
findings.detail: markAttemptFailed only increments attempts and leaves the row PENDING. claimDeliverable has no failure-class, retry-eligibility, attempt-limit, or next-attempt condition, so a permanent error such as a missing target address is retried on every delivery tick indefinitely. Section 34.1 permits retry only when the failure class and idempotency allow it.
findings.suggestedFix: Record a typed failure class and retry decision, use bounded backoff via nextAttemptAt, and move non-retryable or exhausted messages to a terminal rejected state.

findings.summary: Messages targeting terminal or nonexistent sessions remain deliverable
findings.detail: The deliverability query joins only the active role key and generation; it does not join target_session_id to sessions or inspect lifecycle. Call sequence: bind READY session S → transition S to ERROR or STOPPED while its assignment remains ACTIVE → enqueue or retain a pending message → claimDeliverable returns it, and the retained Buzz address can still be used. An arbitrary nonexistent target also passes enqueue and the same query. This routes or loses messages after the runtime is no longer valid.
findings.suggestedFix: Require the target session to exist and have an allowed lifecycle when enqueuing and claiming. Atomically fence active bindings and pending messages when a session enters ERROR or STOPPED.
